newsitem.title: FRANCE: Stars, glitterati shine at lacklustre Cannes run.
newsitem.headline: Stars, glitterati shine at lacklustre Cannes run.

text.p: Halfway into the Cannes festival, no clear favourite emerged on Monday for the Golden Palm award in a largely uninspiring competition eclipsed by the glitter of stars celebrating the 50th edition.

In an attempt to escape a competition diet heavy on dark, violent tales, festival-goers hope Stephan Elliott's "Welcome to Woop Woop" will provide some zany Australian light relief at a midnight screening on Tuesday.

Critics' polls by industry magazines Moving Pictures and Le Film Francais have "Welcome To Sarajevo" by Britain's Michael Winterbottom, based on the true story of a journalist's adoption of a Bosnian girl, and oddball road movie "Western" by France's Manuel Poirier in a narrow lead for the prize-giving.

Last year's winners of the Golden Palm and runner-up jury prize, "Secrets and Lies" by Mike Leigh and "Breaking the Waves" by Lars von Trier, had emerged as outright favourites even before the festival had passed the halfway mark.

Two debut films by leading actors screened in competition, Gary Oldman's brooding "Nil By Mouth" on his East London roots and Johnny Depp's Luciferian "The Brave" on a loser's suicide, won a mixed reception although Depp's understated acting, and a brief appearance by Marlon Brando, earned plaudits.

Maverick American director Abel Ferrara failed to live up to his name for controversy in "The Blackout" starring Matthew Modine, Beatrice Dalle and Claudia Schiffer which did however cause a critics' crush.

But this year, with 50th anniversary celebrations to blame, the May 7-18 extravaganza has been memorable more for glamour and the tributes in which the film industry loves to indulge than for outstanding movies.

When the French Riviera resort invited a bevvy of silver screen greats to Sunday night's birthday celebration, "there was a star climbing the steps of the Palais des Festivals every 45 seconds", in the words of one Cannes organiser.

Sylvester Stallone gave a Rocky-style salute and thrusted past a barrage of security guards to shake hands in the crowd, to be followed up the red carpet by Sigourney Weaver, Martin Scorsese, John Hurt, Hugh Grant and Elizabeth Hurley, and dozens more.
In a moving scene, some 30 previous winners of the Golden Palm award gathered on the stage before a huge mirror which reflected the audience giving them a standing ovation.
Swedish master Ingmar Bergman, who stayed away, was honoured with a special Palm of Palms attributed by his peers before the premiere of Wim Wenders' "The End of Violence".

Last week, cheering crowds had packed the seafront Croisette boulevard to see Michael Jackson present the short movie "Ghosts" in which he features, and Britain's hit-singers the Spice Girls unveil plans for their first film.

Among the most eagerly-awaited entries in the competition are "The Truce" by Italy's Francesco Rosi based on Primo Levi's classic tale of a Nazi death camp survivor's odyssey through Europe, and "The Destiny" by Egypt's Youssef Chahine, which almost failed to be ready in time.
Slap-in-the-face French director Mathieu Kassovitz, who rocked Cannes with the gritty and provocatory "Hatred", is tipped to do more of the same on Friday with "Assassin(s)" starring Michel Serrault.
